one_liner: Theory shows random fermion-photon couplings can enhance, rather than suppress, superradiant order in cavities.
why_it_matters: Disorder is usually treated as harmful, but here it creates a collective regime with many coherent grey states and stronger scaling.
detailed_summary: The work studies fermions coupled to a cavity mode through a random all-to-all interaction matrix with tunable mean and variance. Mean-field numerics, analytic stability theory, random-matrix predictions, and exact-diagonalization benchmarks show that mean coupling and disorder similarly affect the transition onset. Inside the condensed phase, disorder recruits many grey fermionic states coherently, producing parametrically enhanced condensate scaling compared with a single Dicke bright mode.
main_result: Random coupling variance can drive a distinct superradiant phase with enhanced system-size scaling of the cavity condensate.
application_angle: The result points to disorder engineering as a route to stronger collective optical responses in many-body photonic platforms.

title: Theory and practice of Trotter product formulas for quantum chemistry
abstract: Trotter product formulas are a fundamental class of methods for Hamiltonian simulation, particularly attractive due to their low qubit requirements. However, they are often overlooked for use with fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, because of their perceived higher gate counts and the difficulty of estimating Trotter error. Here, we introduce Symmetry-Protected Randomized near-Integrable Trotter (SPRINT) formulas, a framework for building optimized product formulas for electronic structure Hamiltonians widely used in quantum chemistry. SPRINT integrates a generalization of classical near-integrability, randomization, symmetry protection, use of QROM, and other techniques into a thoroughly optimized methodology for Hamiltonian simulation. When applied to concrete simulation tasks, we find SPRINT leads to substantial reduction in gate count compared to previous approaches. Alongside SPRINT, we introduce and analyze a Generalized Rank Decomposition (GRADE) of electronic Hamiltonians that generalizes previous factorization methods. We apply these techniques to the task of simulating the X-ray absorption spectrum of Li$_4$Mn$_2$O, a candidate battery cathode material, leveraging recent advances in tight Trotter error estimation to carefully identify the best version of SPRINT for this problem. Using a Trotter error estimation tool developed in the PennyLane software platform, we show that SPRINT reduces the Toffoli gate cost by a factor of $4.5$ relative to the previous state of the art for this problem, with a gate cost only $\times 2.5$ higher than qubitization, while requiring a dramatic $\times 5.5$ fewer logical qubits. These results establish well-designed Trotter product formulas as an attractive Hamiltonian simulation method for industrially relevant problems in chemistry and materials science.
one_liner: SPRINT product formulas cut fault-tolerant quantum-chemistry simulation cost while using far fewer logical qubits than qubitization.
why_it_matters: It makes Trotter simulation a credible hardware-conscious option for industrial chemistry and materials workloads.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces Symmetry-Protected Randomized near-Integrable Trotter formulas, combining near-integrability, randomization, symmetry protection, QROM, and optimized electronic-structure decompositions. It also presents GRADE, a generalized rank decomposition for electronic Hamiltonians. For simulating the X-ray absorption spectrum of Li4Mn2O, SPRINT reduces Toffoli cost by 4.5x versus the previous state of the art while using 5.5x fewer logical qubits than qubitization.
main_result: SPRINT achieves a 4.5x Toffoli reduction for a battery-cathode simulation task, with cost only 2.5x above qubitization and much lower qubit demand.
application_angle: The method improves the resource tradeoff for practical fault-tolerant simulations of chemistry and materials relevant to industry.

title: Adaptive Eigenvector Continuation for Full-Vector Photonic Waveguide Mode Emulation
abstract: Photonic waveguide design often requires repeated full-vector Maxwell eigenmode solves over wavelength, geometry, and material parameters. We present an adaptive eigenvector-continuation framework for accelerating and stabilizing these modal sweeps. The method constructs a reduced basis from selected full-order modal snapshots, solves projected Maxwell eigenproblems at new query points, reconstructs the modal fields, and monitors accuracy with a full operator residual. We demonstrate three regimes. In fixed-geometry wavelength sweeps of a strip waveguide, well-distributed snapshots reproduce the target modal branch with low residual and low effective-index error. In a multimode ridge waveguide, a shared reduced basis containing several modal families enables robust broadband mode-family tracking and residual-guided adaptive enrichment. In geometry-dependent width sweeps, the method gives accurate effective-index predictions and high field overlap, but the residual reveals moving-boundary errors caused by non-smooth changes of the discrete operator on a fixed Cartesian grid. These results show that adaptive eigenvector continuation is an operator-consistent modal emulator and diagnostic tool for photonic waveguide sweeps.
one_liner: Adaptive eigenvector continuation accelerates full-vector photonic waveguide mode sweeps with residual-based error checks.
why_it_matters: Fast, stable modal emulation can reduce repeated Maxwell solves in photonic design loops across wavelength and geometry.
detailed_summary: The method builds a reduced basis from full-order modal snapshots, solves projected Maxwell eigenproblems at query points, reconstructs fields, and evaluates a full operator residual. Demonstrations cover strip-waveguide wavelength sweeps, multimode ridge-waveguide broadband tracking, and geometry-dependent width sweeps. The residual also diagnoses moving-boundary errors from non-smooth discrete-operator changes on a fixed Cartesian grid.
main_result: The framework reproduces modal branches with low effective-index error and high field overlap while adaptively enriching the basis when residuals grow.
application_angle: It can speed photonic component optimization and provide diagnostics for wavelength, multimode, and geometry sweeps.

title: Revivals of Bell nonlocality require Schrödinger and Heisenberg non-Markovianity
abstract: Bell nonlocality is a key resource in quantum information, demonstrating the nonclassicality of quantum theory. Noise, however, {is in general detrimental to} nonlocality, and can cause the loss of the ability to violate any Bell inequality. Memory effects, on the other hand, can restore {this} quantumness and, as recently shown, they can be {differently characterized} in the Schrödinger and in the Heisenberg picture. Here, we show that if memory effects allow for revivals in time of nonlocality, then the dynamics must be non-Markovian in both pictures. We showcase our findings through a device-independent quantum key distribution task, for which Bell nonlocality is necessary.
one_liner: Bell-nonlocality revivals are shown to require non-Markovian memory in both Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures.
why_it_matters: The result links a device-independent communication resource to stringent dynamical memory conditions under noise.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes when noisy dynamics can restore the ability to violate Bell inequalities after nonlocality has been lost. It proves that such revivals require non-Markovianity in both the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, reflecting memory effects in state and observable evolution. The authors illustrate the implication using a device-independent quantum key distribution task where Bell nonlocality is necessary.
main_result: Any time revival of Bell nonlocality implies non-Markovian dynamics in both pictures.
application_angle: It clarifies when environmental memory can restore resources needed for device-independent secure communication.

title: Improving the loss threshold for quantum advantage in photonic sensors by complete photon counting
abstract: Tolerance to imperfections is a defining performance criterion for quantum sensors. The threshold for achieving a quantum advantage depends on the input state, sensor configuration, detection scheme, and, critically for optical platforms, photon loss. We consider a nonlinear interferometer in which two gain-optimized parametric nonlinear optical processes couple the state to the internal sensor and subsequently mix the reference and sensor beams. We demonstrate that measuring the full photon-number output statistics of this setup yields marked improvements in the loss threshold. Using photon-number-resolving detection (PNRD) based on transition-edge sensors (TESs), we experimentally reconstruct the joint photon-number statistics at the interferometer output. Subject to internal and external losses of approximately 25 % and 45 %, respectively -- and without any post-selection or loss correction -- we observe an unconditional violation of the shot-noise limit by $2.37 \pm 0.11$ dB. This translates to a 44 % enhancement in estimation precision over conventional click-detection strategies. We verify this performance by evaluating the classical Fisher information against both an analytical model of the joint photon-number distribution and the raw measured statistics. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that combining nonlinear interferometry with PNRD unlocks metrological information fundamentally inaccessible to click detectors, establishing a clear path toward practical, quantum-enhanced sensing under realistic loss conditions.
one_liner: Complete photon counting in a nonlinear interferometer beats the shot-noise limit despite substantial optical loss.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows photon-number-resolving detection can recover metrological information missed by click detectors under realistic loss.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses a nonlinear interferometer with gain-optimized parametric optical processes and transition-edge-sensor photon-number-resolving detection. By reconstructing joint photon-number output statistics, the authors evaluate classical Fisher information from both measured data and an analytical distribution model. With about 25% internal loss and 45% external loss, they report an unconditional 2.37 +/- 0.11 dB violation of the shot-noise limit without post-selection or loss correction.
main_result: Full photon-number statistics deliver a 44% precision improvement over click-detection strategies under high loss.
application_angle: The result supports practical quantum-enhanced optical sensing using loss-tolerant readout rather than idealized detection assumptions.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Individual Atomic Control and Cooling
abstract: Real-time feedback control of quantum systems is often limited by partial observations, nonlinear dynamics and measurement noise, which make accurate model-based controllers difficult to design. Here we show that deep reinforcement learning can cool the motion of a single neutral atom coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity using only the continuously monitored cavity transmission. We first train the controller in simulation and then transfer it to the experiment, where online fine-tuning adapts it to unmodeled experimental dynamics. The learned policy damps the atom's motion in real time and achieves a cooling time constant of 388 +/- 14 microseconds, corresponding to only two motional periods in the trap. It also outperforms a standard linear differentiator controller in cooling speed while maintaining comparable atom retention over a broad range of operating conditions. These results establish reinforcement learning as a practical strategy for feedback control in quantum-limited experiments where compact analytical models are incomplete.
one_liner: Deep RL cools a single cavity-coupled neutral atom using real-time transmission feedback and experiment-side fine tuning.
why_it_matters: It shows learned controllers can outperform simple analytical feedback in noisy, partially observed quantum hardware experiments.
detailed_summary: The work trains a deep reinforcement-learning controller in simulation to act on continuously monitored optical-cavity transmission from a trapped neutral atom. After transfer to the lab, online fine tuning adapts the policy to unmodeled dynamics and measurement noise. The controller damps atomic motion with a 388 +/- 14 us cooling time constant, about two motional periods, while maintaining atom retention across operating conditions.
platform_or_system: single neutral atom in optical cavity
main_result: A learned feedback policy achieved real-time atom cooling faster than a standard linear differentiator controller.
application_angle: Adaptive feedback of this kind could improve tuning, stabilization, and operation of neutral-atom quantum processors and cavity-QED devices.

title: CryoZip: An Efficient Cryogenic Compressor for Quantum Error Correction Syndromes
abstract: Scaling fault tolerant quantum computing is increasingly constrained by the limited bandwidth and power budget across the 4 K to room temperature (RT) interface. We present CryoZip, a cross stack cryogenic compression framework that cooperates with a lightweight cryogenic quantum error correction (QEC) predecoder to reduce 4 K to RT syndrome transmission under realistic, circuit level noise. CryoZip targets sparse syndrome vectors with a sliding window compression architecture sized under strict decoding latency constraints to maximize energy efficiency. We implement and evaluate the design in 22 nm FDSOI characterized at 4 K, using vector based power, performance, and area analysis to obtain realistic hardware data. CryoZip achieves up to 48x compression, 1.8x higher than state of the art compressors, across various QEC codes while delivering 4 to 26x energy savings. When paired with a QEC predecoder, it yields over 14,238x bandwidth reduction, while energy savings rise to 42x when accounting for realistic QEC interface overheads.
one_liner: CryoZip compresses sparse QEC syndrome streams at 4 K to ease the bandwidth and energy bottleneck to room-temperature decoders.
why_it_matters: Cryogenic data movement is a major scaling constraint for fault-tolerant quantum computers, and syndrome compression attacks it directly.
detailed_summary: CryoZip is a cross-stack compression architecture co-designed with a lightweight cryogenic QEC predecoder for sparse circuit-level syndrome vectors. The design uses sliding-window compression sized to satisfy decoding-latency constraints and is evaluated with 22 nm FDSOI hardware data characterized at 4 K. It reports up to 48x compression, 4 to 26x energy savings, and over 14238x bandwidth reduction when paired with predecoding.
main_result: The framework demonstrates large syndrome bandwidth reduction and energy savings under realistic circuit-level noise and cryogenic hardware assumptions.
application_angle: This could reduce wiring, power, and data-transfer pressure in scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing systems.

title: Rethinking quantum information in gravity and fields
abstract: This paper presents a curated selection of research questions at the intersection of quantum gravity and quantum information, chosen to highlight issues that we regard as particularly important for researchers in both fields. We organize the discussion into four main themes: the operational characterization of observables, the role of observers, quantum error correction, and the infinite-dimensionality of Hilbert spaces. We hope that addressing these questions will engage researchers across both communities and further strengthen the profound interplay between the two disciplines.
one_liner: A perspective maps research questions linking quantum information, observables, observers, QEC, and field-theoretic Hilbert spaces.
why_it_matters: It clarifies conceptual targets where quantum information ideas may reshape gravity and field-theory hardware abstractions.
detailed_summary: The paper is a curated perspective rather than an experimental demonstration. It organizes open problems around operational observables, the role of observers, quantum error correction, and infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The emphasis is on sharpening questions that connect quantum-information primitives to gravity and quantum fields.
main_result: The main contribution is a structured agenda of open problems at the quantum information and gravity interface.
application_angle: Its relevance is indirect, by framing QEC and operational-observable ideas that may inform future quantum simulation and hardware theory.

title: Overcoming Configuration Bottleneck: Modular Pathways to Stable Semiconductor Spin-Qubit Arrays
abstract: Over the past decade, semiconductor spin qubits have progressed from few-qubit demonstrations towards larger-scale devices fabricated in increasingly reproducible academic and industrial processes. This progress marks an inflection point: the central challenge is no longer to demonstrate high-fidelity operation in carefully tuned devices, but to discover, verify, and maintain stable operating conditions reliably across many interdependent controls, varied device geometries, and disparate material platforms. In this Perspective, we frame spin-qubit operation as a modular automation problem. We decompose the workflow into five modules: bootstrapping from minimal prior information, configuration tuning, virtualization of physical gates into effective control axes, qubit-level tuning, and an operation layer with drift-aware maintenance. Using recent demonstrations from our work and the broader community, we argue that scalability will depend on explicit interfaces between modules, standardized intermediate data products, and workflow-level metrics such as throughput, success probability, stability time, recovery time, and robustness. We close by outlining the infrastructure needed to move beyond isolated tuning demonstrations toward sustained operation: qubit-performance-aware feedback, reusable software and benchmark tasks, and tight collaboration among experimental, theoretical, and software efforts.
one_liner: A perspective frames scalable semiconductor spin-qubit operation as a modular, automated tuning and maintenance workflow.
why_it_matters: Large spin-qubit arrays need reliable configuration discovery and drift recovery, not just isolated high-fidelity demonstrations.
detailed_summary: The paper decomposes spin-qubit operation into modules for bootstrapping, configuration tuning, gate virtualization, qubit-level tuning, and drift-aware operation. It argues that explicit interfaces, standardized intermediate data, and workflow metrics are required for scaling across devices and material platforms. Proposed metrics include throughput, success probability, stability time, recovery time, and robustness.
main_result: The work provides a modular automation blueprint for discovering, verifying, and maintaining stable spin-qubit operating points.
application_angle: The framework targets a practical bottleneck in deploying many-qubit semiconductor processors with sustained autonomous operation.

title: Quantum Imaging via Kurtosis-Difference Weighted Covariance on 2D Camera
abstract: Camera-based quantum imaging detects spatially correlated photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). Conventional covariance methods typically require tens of thousands of frames to extract weak correlations from noise. While thick crystals can increase photon flux, they generate photon pairs from multiple emission positions within the crystal, producing multiple correlation centers with complex pairing geometries. In addition, conventional covariance methods assume a single pre-selected correlation center and cannot fully exploit these distributed correlations. We demonstrate that kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic measuring tail similarity, effectively discriminates correlated pixel pairs even when correlation coefficients remain low. Weighting covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference can select symmetric pixels while preserving true coincidences. This kurtosis weighting automatically identifies correlated pairs within a broad search region and accommodates multiple pairing geometries without requiring precise correlation center calibration. At 5000 frames, our method yields a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) exceeding 7, whereas standard covariance remains below 2. Compared with standard covariance, the method reduces the acquisition time by 40-fold and could enable practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.
one_liner: Kurtosis-difference weighted covariance extracts SPDC photon-pair correlations from far fewer camera frames than standard covariance.
why_it_matters: Reducing acquisition time makes camera-based quantum imaging more practical in sparse correlated-photon regimes.
detailed_summary: The method uses kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic, to identify pixel pairs with similar heavy-tailed photon-count behavior even when linear correlations are weak. It weights covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference, allowing automatic selection of symmetric correlated pixels over broad search regions. At 5000 frames it achieves CNR above 7, while standard covariance remains below 2, corresponding to a reported 40-fold acquisition-time reduction.
main_result: The technique recovers distributed spatial photon-pair correlations with much higher CNR at low frame counts than standard covariance.
application_angle: It could support faster low-light quantum imaging, correlation microscopy, and sensing systems using camera-detected photon pairs.

title: Spin-Squeezing-Enhanced Charging for Quantum Dicke Batteries
abstract: High-power Dicke quantum batteries (QBs) typically exploit collective superradiance, whereas intrinsic matter-matter interactions are conventionally considered detrimental. Here, we propose a counterintuitive paradigm: these interactions can be controlled and repurposed as a synergistic resource to enhance charging power and capacity. In the low-excitation limit, transverse interactions induce collective spin squeezing, causing critical mode softening and an exponential enhancement of effective coupling, which significantly boosts charging power. At higher excitations, these interactions act as a macroscopic nonlinear torque. By appropriately aligning this torque, we effectively lower phase-space dynamical barriers, guiding the system along optimal rapid-charging paths. Importantly, this cooperative enhancement remains highly robust under realistic dissipation, outperforming ideal, dissipationless Dicke QBs in specific regimes. Our results provide a blueprint for exploiting matter interactions to design dissipation-resistant, high-performance many-body QBs.
one_liner: Controlled matter-matter interactions enhance Dicke quantum-battery charging through spin squeezing and nonlinear phase-space dynamics.
why_it_matters: It turns interactions usually treated as harmful into a resource for robust, high-power many-body quantum energy storage.
detailed_summary: The theory proposes using transverse matter-matter interactions to improve Dicke quantum-battery charging rather than suppressing them. In the low-excitation limit, the interactions generate collective spin squeezing, mode softening, and enhanced effective coupling. At higher excitation, they provide a nonlinear torque that can guide the system along faster charging trajectories and remain robust under realistic dissipation.
main_result: The paper predicts interaction-assisted charging power and capacity improvements, including regimes outperforming ideal dissipationless Dicke batteries.
application_angle: The concept may guide photonic or collective-spin platforms for high-power quantum batteries and engineered many-body energy devices.

title: Continuous-Variable Source-Independent Quantum Random Number Generation with General POVMs
abstract: Continuous-variable source-independent quantum random number generators offer the highest generation rates among semi-device-independent protocols. In reality, the protocol design is limited due to permissible measurement configurations. In this work, we propose a rigorous security proof framework that accommodates general, infinite-dimensional positive-operator-valued measures. Building upon the numerical security proof framework, we evaluate the randomness lower bound by maximizing the eavesdropper's guessing probability. Specifically, we transform the inherently infinite-dimensional semidefinite program in Fock space into a tractable finite-dimensional one, rigorously proving that latter provides a strict upper bound to the guessing probability of the original infinite-dimensional problem. Our framework showcases its capability by certifying secure randomness using unbalanced homodyne detection with only a single quadrature measurement, thereby bypassing the traditional requirement of measuring two conjugate quadratures such as $X$ and $P$. We experimentally validate our protocol on an optical platform using vacuum and weak coherent states, achieving a maximum secure randomness extraction of 1.11 bits per sample and an ultra-high generation rate of 1.776 Gbps. This work provides a flexible design for practical, high-speed quantum random number generators.
one_liner: A source-independent CV QRNG security framework supports general POVMs and reaches 1.776 Gbps on an optical setup.
why_it_matters: It relaxes measurement-design constraints for practical semi-device-independent QRNGs while preserving finite-dimensional, rigorous security certification.
detailed_summary: The work builds a security proof for continuous-variable source-independent QRNGs with general infinite-dimensional POVMs. It converts the Fock-space guessing-probability SDP into a finite-dimensional problem that upper-bounds the original eavesdropper advantage. The experiment uses vacuum and weak coherent states with unbalanced homodyne detection and only one measured quadrature, extracting up to 1.11 secure bits per sample.
main_result: The protocol certifies secure randomness with single-quadrature unbalanced homodyne detection and demonstrates a 1.776 Gbps secure generation rate.
application_angle: The result points to simpler, faster, and more flexible quantum random-number generators for cryptography and secure communications.

title: Phase space quantization of anisotropic cosmologies: Taub and Kantowski-Sachs models
abstract: We introduce an explicit construction of the non-diagonal and diagonal Wigner distributions for the homogeneous but anisotropic Taub and Kantowski-Sachs cosmological models within the framework of phase space deformation quantization. Conventional canonical quantization of these models via the Wheeler-DeWitt equation is inherently plagued by factor ordering ambiguities. To circumvent these issues, we employ the totally symmetric Weyl quantization map and the Moyal star product. By means of a canonical separation of the Hamiltonian constraint, we are able to resolve the formal convergence problems typically associated with the star product. Furthermore, to establish a rigorous connection with conventional quantum cosmology, we calculate the standard wave functions directly from the diagonal Wigner distributions, recovering the exact physical states in terms of modified Bessel functions in both cases.
one_liner: A phase-space quantization method constructs Wigner distributions for Taub and Kantowski-Sachs anisotropic cosmologies.
why_it_matters: It provides a factor-ordering-free quantization route and recovers exact physical wave functions, but is mainly theoretical rather than device-facing.
detailed_summary: The paper applies deformation quantization to homogeneous anisotropic Taub and Kantowski-Sachs cosmological models. Using Weyl quantization and the Moyal star product, it avoids Wheeler-DeWitt factor-ordering ambiguities and handles convergence through canonical separation of the Hamiltonian constraint. Diagonal Wigner distributions are then used to reconstruct standard wave functions in terms of modified Bessel functions.
main_result: The authors explicitly construct diagonal and non-diagonal Wigner distributions and recover the exact physical states for both models.
application_angle: Its relevance is methodological, offering phase-space tools that may inform quantum simulation or theoretical treatments of constrained quantum systems.

title: Generalised quantum interference
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is one of the clearest signatures of quantum behaviour: two identical photons meeting at a beam splitter always leave together. Here we demonstrate that this symmetry can be broken. Using a programmable integrated photonic processor, we interfere imbalanced two-photon states on a variable beam splitter and show that the output state of quantum interference can be continuously tuned, reaching the extreme case where destructive interference suppresses bunching at one output port. The asymmetry creates a forbidden bunching channel: photons may exit together at one port or separately at both ports, but cannot emerge together at the other port.
one_liner: Programmable integrated photonics tunes two-photon interference into asymmetric output channels beyond standard HOM behavior.
why_it_matters: It expands controllable multiphoton interference primitives on chip, a core ingredient for photonic quantum information processing.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses a programmable integrated photonic processor to interfere imbalanced two-photon states on a tunable beam splitter. Unlike conventional Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, the output symmetry can be continuously broken. At the extreme setting, destructive interference suppresses bunching in one port, leaving only the opposite bunching channel or coincidence outcomes.
main_result: The team demonstrates continuously tunable asymmetric two-photon interference with a forbidden bunching channel at one output port.
application_angle: This gives photonic circuits a finer interference-control primitive for quantum gates, state preparation, and bosonic information processing.

title: Floquet Quasienergy-Resolved Dissipation, Dynamics, and Spectroscopy in Ultrastrong Cavity-QED
abstract: Strong periodic driving of cavity-quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the ultrastrong-coupling regime creates nonequilibrium states whose dissipation is governed by Floquet quasienergies rather than undriven dressed resonances. However, modeling such a regime is a significant theoretical challenge, including a number of subtle problems such as the need to ensure gauge invariance for truncated matter-cavity systems with time-dependent driving. To fill this theoretical gap, we introduce a nonsecular Floquet generalized master equation framework for strongly driven open cavity-QED systems, formulated in the dressed basis of the quantum Rabi model and applicable to structured reservoirs without rotating-wave approximations. Our theory can thus model Floquet-driven dynamics in open ultrastrong-coupling cavity-QED, and demonstrates a wide range of quantum state control. Using strong optical pumping and parametric mechanical modulation, we compute long-time populations, fluorescence spectra, and the Floquet-Liouville eigenspectra, resolving observable resonances into hybridized quasienergy channels and decay rates. By systematically comparing with conventional time-independent dressed-basis generalized master equations, we show that static approaches only reproduce steady-state populations in restricted excitation regimes, and fail for frequency-resolved observables and break down under appropriate Floquet engineering, surprisingly, even for spectrally flat baths. Structured environments, such as Lorentzian-Ohmic reservoirs, further amplify these discrepancies through sideband-selective decay. Our results demonstrate that dissipation in driven ultrastrong cavity-QED is intrinsically quasienergy resolved and we establish Floquet-dissipative theory as an accurate and powerful framework for predicting spectra, controlling decay pathways, and engineering nonequilibrium quantum states and reservoirs.
one_liner: A nonsecular Floquet master-equation framework predicts quasienergy-resolved dissipation in driven ultrastrong cavity QED.
why_it_matters: It supplies the modeling needed to engineer spectra, decay pathways, and nonequilibrium states in strongly driven cavity-QED hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a gauge-aware, nonsecular Floquet generalized master equation in the dressed basis of the quantum Rabi model. It treats strong periodic driving, structured reservoirs, and open-system dynamics without rotating-wave approximations. Calculations of populations, fluorescence spectra, and Floquet-Liouville eigenspectra show that static dressed-basis approaches miss frequency-resolved observables and can fail even for flat baths under Floquet engineering.
main_result: The framework resolves observable resonances into hybridized quasienergy channels and decay rates under strong optical and parametric driving.
application_angle: It enables predictive design of driven cavity-QED devices for quantum state control, reservoir engineering, and spectroscopy.

title: Radical-Fragment Many-Body Expansion for Linear Alkane Quantum Chemistry
abstract: We introduce a radical-fragment many-body expansion at the two-body level (MBE2) for quantum chemistry of linear alkanes. Instead of heterolytic bond cleavage with hydrogen capping atoms and electrostatic embedding like in Fragment Molecular Orbital (FMO), we perform homolytic C-C bond cleavage to produce open-shell radical fragments (CH3, CH2) treated with restricted open-shell Hartree-Fock (ROHF) in isolation. The two-body MBE2 assembly formula reconstructs total alkane energies from only four unique fragment calculations regardless of chain length, reducing the maximum qubit requirement. We benchmark this framework against five energy solvers (RHF, CCSD, VQE, ADAPT-VQE, and SQD) across 11 linear alkanes from butane (C4H10) to hexacosane (C26H54). The MBE2 decomposition achieves a 12.3x qubit reduction for C26H54 (from 368 to 30 qubits) and a 12.8x reduction in unique calculations via symmetry exploitation. MBE2-VQE and MBE2-SQD (executed on IBM quantum hardware) closely track their respective classical MBE2 references, demonstrating that fragmentation-based quantum chemistry is viable for scaling quantum solvers to large molecular systems.
one_liner: Radical-fragment MBE2 cuts alkane quantum-chemistry qubit needs and is tested with VQE, ADAPT-VQE, SQD, and IBM hardware.
why_it_matters: It shows a concrete path to scaling molecular quantum chemistry workloads by reducing active qubits through chemically structured fragmentation.
detailed_summary: The method fragments linear alkanes by homolytic C-C cleavage into open-shell radical fragments treated with ROHF, then reconstructs energies using a two-body many-body expansion. Because only four unique fragment calculations are needed regardless of chain length, the resource count drops substantially. Benchmarks across C4H10 to C26H54 include classical solvers and quantum solvers, with MBE2-SQD executed on IBM quantum hardware.
main_result: For C26H54, the approach reduces the requirement from 368 to 30 qubits and achieves close agreement between quantum-fragment and classical-fragment references.
application_angle: The scheme makes larger molecular energy-estimation problems more accessible to near-term quantum processors.

title: Entanglement Structure Across $\mathbb{Z}_n$ Phase Transitions in 1D Rydberg Atom Arrays
abstract: Multipartite quantum entanglement plays a crucial role in the emergence of different quantum phases and their transitions in quantum many-body systems. It is of general interest to know what sort of analysis on quantum entanglement can bring us a profound insight to understand the rich dynamics of quantum many-body systems. In this work we study the characteristics of quantum entanglement in relation to $\mathbb{Z}_n$-ordered phases emerging under a varied strength of 1-dim Rydberg interaction. We propose an approach based on the structure of pair-wise entanglement across the Rydberg chain using two-qubit concurrence as an entanglement measure. We define an entanglement-structure factor via Fourier analysis of total concurrence at each site and address $\mathbb{Z}_n$ phase transitions in comparison with the conventional order-parameter based on local density, i.e. magnetization. We also discuss how the required two-qubit concurrence can be measured in analog Rydberg atom arrays using site-selective erasure and parametrized laser pulses. Our investigation suggests that an entanglement-structure-based approach can provide a powerful tool in analyzing symmetry-breaking in quantum phase transitions.
one_liner: Pairwise-concurrence structure factors diagnose Zn phase transitions in 1D Rydberg atom arrays.
why_it_matters: It proposes experimentally accessible entanglement observables for identifying ordered phases in analog quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes multipartite entanglement across symmetry-breaking Zn-ordered phases in one-dimensional Rydberg chains. It defines an entanglement-structure factor by Fourier-analyzing site-resolved total two-qubit concurrence and compares it with conventional density-based order parameters. The authors also outline measurement using site-selective erasure and parametrized laser pulses in analog Rydberg arrays.
main_result: The proposed concurrence-based structure factor tracks Zn phase transitions and offers information complementary to local magnetization.
application_angle: The approach could improve diagnostics and benchmarking of programmable Rydberg quantum simulators used for many-body physics and hardware validation.

title: Unresolved-Sideband Optomechanics with Hexagonal Boron Nitride: Induced Transparency, Gain, and Frequency Combs
abstract: Optomechanically induced transparency (OMIT) is usually modeled and studied in the resolved-sideband regime, but many compact microcavity platforms operate in the unresolved-sideband limit $(κ\gg Ω_m)$. Here we investigate OMIT in this regime using a tunable fiber-based Fabry-Perot microcavity coupled to a suspended hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) drum resonator in a membrane-in-the-middle geometry. The system achieves a large single-photon coupling rate of $g_0/2π\sim 180$ kHz and exhibits strong radiation-pressure backaction. By measuring OMIT spectra as a function of pump power and cavity detuning, we observe a crossover from a transparency-like dip to a gain feature in the reflected response. These maps are quantitatively reproduced by the full linearized optomechanical response, demonstrating the breakdown of the standard rotating-wave approximation used in the resolved-sideband limit. Finally, we drive the system into a nonlinear regime to generate optomechanical frequency combs. These results establish hBN fiber-cavities as a versatile architecture for unresolved-sideband optomechanics, nonlinear dynamics, and hybrid device integration.
one_liner: hBN drum-in-cavity optomechanics shows unresolved-sideband OMIT, gain crossover, and nonlinear frequency-comb generation.
why_it_matters: It validates compact hBN fiber microcavities as a strong-coupling platform where standard resolved-sideband approximations fail but useful nonlinear photonics emerges.
detailed_summary: The work studies a suspended hexagonal boron nitride drum in a tunable fiber Fabry-Perot membrane-in-the-middle cavity operating with kappa much larger than the mechanical frequency. With single-photon coupling around g0/2pi = 180 kHz, pump-power and detuning maps show a transition from transparency-like response to gain in reflection. The data are reproduced by the full linearized optomechanical response, exposing the breakdown of the rotating-wave approximation, and nonlinear driving generates optomechanical frequency combs.
main_result: The system demonstrates unresolved-sideband OMIT-to-gain crossover and optomechanical frequency-comb generation with strong radiation-pressure backaction.
application_angle: Compact hBN optomechanics is relevant for integrated nonlinear photonics, hybrid sensors, and chip-compatible cavity-mechanical devices.

title: Mapping photon-number regimes in single-emitter lasers
abstract: Cavity quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architectures are known to produce traditional laser signatures from a coherently driven single quantum emitter. In this paper, we present a numerical analysis of an open quantum system consisting of an incoherently pumped three-level emitter strongly coupled to a single cavity mode. In particular, we focus on three cavity photon-number ($n_p$) regimes modeled within a truncated Hilbert space of dimension up to $N=51$: deep quantum ($n_p \leq 1$), intermediate quantum ($2 \leq n_p \leq 50$), and semi-classical ($n_p \gg 50$). We investigate the photon threshold for entering the lasing regime while completely bypassing the requirement for a coherent drive, revealing that laser behavior can emerge from minimal photon populations. For example, by solving the Lindblad master equation, we find that lasing stabilizes in the intermediate quantum regime where stimulated emission dominates spontaneous emission. We further observe sub-Poissonian photon statistics in this regime, as confirmed by a donut-like Wigner distribution, near-unity second-order coherence function $g^{(2)}(0) \approx 1$, and a minimized Mandel $Q$-parameter. However, within the range $10 < n_p < 50$, we observe a loss of coherence at higher incoherent pumping rates, leading to self-quenching. In the semi-classical regime ($n_p \gg 50$), treated under a mean-field approximation for our choice of system parameters, we find that the laser quenches at an incoherent pumping rate of $Γ\approx 65$ (in units of the atomic decay rate $γ_{12}$). Our findings can be applied to define the operational limits of single-emitter light sources, thereby providing useful guidelines for the development of nanolasers and scalable quantum networks.
one_liner: Numerics map photon-number regimes where an incoherently pumped single-emitter cavity can lase with few photons before self-quenching.
why_it_matters: It gives design limits for nanolasers and single-emitter quantum-network light sources without requiring coherent drive operation.
detailed_summary: The paper numerically analyzes an incoherently pumped three-level emitter strongly coupled to one cavity mode, using truncated Hilbert spaces up to dimension 51 and mean-field treatment at high photon number. It separates deep quantum, intermediate quantum, and semiclassical regimes and identifies lasing onset when stimulated emission dominates spontaneous emission. In the intermediate regime it finds near-unity g2(0), minimized Mandel Q, sub-Poissonian statistics, and a donut-like Wigner distribution, followed by coherence loss and self-quenching at stronger pumping.
main_result: The model shows that laser-like operation can stabilize at photon numbers between 2 and 50 under incoherent pumping, but quenches at higher pump rates.
application_angle: The regime map informs practical operating windows for nanoscale light sources used in sensing and scalable quantum communication nodes.

title: Absorption capacity of separable noise: Bell-mixing thresholds on separability and teleportation
abstract: We study Bell-mixing lines $ρ_λ=λΦ^+ +(1-λ)σ$, where $Φ^+$ is a fixed Bell reference and $σ$ is a separable two-qubit noise state. Along this line there are two operational crossings: the state becomes entangled, and it reaches quantum teleportation advantage over classical strategies. We package these crossings as capacities of the noise state. The entanglement absorption capacity $C_{\rm abs}(σ)$ is the largest amount of Bell reference that $σ$ can absorb while the partial transpose remains positive. The fidelity absorption capacity $C_F(σ)$ is the largest amount of Bell reference that $σ$ can absorb while keeping the maximal teleportation fidelity at or below the classical bound $2/3$. The thresholds corresponding to the two crossing points are obtained from the same Möbius map, $λ_* = C_{\rm abs}/(1+C_{\rm abs})$ and $λ_F = C_F/(1+C_F)$. We derive closed-form capacities and thresholds for product noise states and separable complex $X$ noise states. For product noise, $C_{\rm abs}$ depends only on local marginal purities, while $C_F$ also depends on orientation relative to the maximally entangled reference. For $X$ noise states, both capacities are explicit in all four Bell frames. We also study three extensions: arbitrary pure-state references, the evolution of $X$ noise states and their capacities under local amplitude-damping and dephasing channels, and decomposition certificates that give lower bounds on the capacities, hence on the thresholds, for general separable noise.
one_liner: The paper derives Bell-mixing thresholds for when separable two-qubit noise becomes entangled or teleportation-useful.
why_it_matters: Closed-form noise absorption capacities give concrete benchmarks for entanglement and teleportation advantage under structured separable noise.
detailed_summary: The work defines entanglement absorption capacity and fidelity absorption capacity for Bell-reference mixing with a separable two-qubit noise state. These capacities determine the Bell-fraction thresholds for losing PPT separability and for exceeding the classical teleportation fidelity bound of 2/3 through a shared Mobius map. Closed forms are derived for product noise and separable complex X states, with extensions to pure-state references, local damping and dephasing, and decomposition certificates for lower bounds.
main_result: It provides analytic separability and teleportation-advantage thresholds for product and X-state separable noise in multiple Bell frames.
application_angle: The thresholds quantify how much entanglement resource is needed to overcome realistic separable noise in teleportation and communication protocols.

title: Ferroelectric transmon
abstract: Superconducting qubits are a leading platform for quantum computing. However, simultaneously achieving low noise sensitivity to suppress decoherence and sufficient anharmonicity to enable fast gate operations remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce the concept of the ferroelectric transmon (FEmon), in which the Josephson junction is shunted by a ferroelectric, or incipient ferroelectric, capacitor. We show, in particular, that the nonlinear ferroelectric response of the capacitor provides an additional degree of freedom for optimizing qubit anharmonicity while preserving operation in the charge-noise-insensitive regime.
one_liner: A ferroelectric-shunted transmon concept adds capacitor nonlinearity to tune anharmonicity while retaining charge-noise protection.
why_it_matters: It proposes a hardware knob for superconducting qubits that could ease the tradeoff between long coherence and fast, spectrally selective gates.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces the ferroelectric transmon, or FEmon, in which a Josephson junction is shunted by a ferroelectric or incipient-ferroelectric capacitor. The nonlinear dielectric response supplies an extra design degree of freedom beyond the usual Josephson and charging energies. The analysis argues this can enhance or optimize qubit anharmonicity while keeping the device in the charge-noise-insensitive transmon regime.
main_result: The proposed FEmon architecture uses nonlinear ferroelectric capacitance to improve anharmonicity without leaving the transmon protection regime.
application_angle: If realized with low loss, the design could support faster gates and denser superconducting-qubit spectra in scalable processors.

title: Full-Wave Green's-Function Modeling of Collective Single-Photon Emission in Non-Markovian Open-System QED with Finite-Bandwidth Compensation of Dispersive Interactions
abstract: This work presents a full-wave Green's function framework for modeling collective and coherent single-photon emission from multiple quantum emitters embedded in complex electromagnetic structures. Starting from a transverse modal completeness relation of modified Langevin noise formalism, we derive a closed set of coupled equations for population dynamics and frequency-resolved field amplitudes in the single-excitation regime. Since the electromagnetic reservoir is not traced out at the level of the dynamical amplitudes, the emitted single-photon dynamics can be modeled within the same closed set of equations without Markovian approximation in open and dissipative environments. We demonstrate that finite-bandwidth truncation of the spectral density leads to systematic deviations in coherent dispersive interactions, even when dissipative rates appear converged. To restore causal consistency, we introduce a counter-term compensation scheme that restores the missing dispersive contributions without modifying the retained non-Markovian memory kernel. To validate the scheme and demonstrate the practicality of the proposed framework, we present numerical examples ranging from benchmark configurations to a three-dimensional dispersive ring-resonator structure via finite element method. These capabilities provide a practical route for rigorously incorporating full-wave electromagnetic simulations into non-Markovian multi-emitter quantum electrodynamics, enabling predictive modeling of collective emission, coherent energy exchange, and single-photon radiation in realistic open structures.
one_liner: A full-wave Green-function framework models non-Markovian collective single-photon emission in realistic open nanophotonic structures.
why_it_matters: It connects finite-element electromagnetics directly to multi-emitter quantum dynamics, improving predictive design of quantum photonic devices.
detailed_summary: The paper derives closed coupled equations for emitter populations and frequency-resolved field amplitudes in the single-excitation regime using a transverse modal completeness relation. Because the reservoir is retained dynamically rather than traced out, the method captures non-Markovian single-photon emission in open, dissipative electromagnetic environments. It also identifies errors from finite-bandwidth spectral truncation and introduces a counter-term compensation scheme that restores missing dispersive interactions while preserving the memory kernel.
main_result: The framework accurately models collective emission, coherent exchange, and emitted single-photon fields in benchmark systems and a 3D dispersive ring resonator.
application_angle: It enables simulation-guided engineering of quantum emitters in cavities, waveguides, and resonators for photonic quantum technologies.

title: Projection Operator Stochastic Equations for Non-Markovian Quantum Systems Under Continuous Measurement-Based Feedback
abstract: Quantum Markov models have been successfully used to accurately model various physical quantum systems in fields such as quantum optics, optomechanics and superconducting circuits and they provide the basis for (measurement-based) quantum feedback control. However, the quantum Markov assumption is a strong one and it is not expected to hold for general quantum systems of interest. The projection operator approach is one approach that has been developed to model non-Markovian quantum systems by considering its embedding in a larger Markovian quantum system, but mainly in the context of quantum master equations for the dynamics of the unmonitored reduced quantum state of a quantum system. This approach was recently adapted for continuously measured non-Markovian quantum systems, which enables open-loop control but did not yet consider the presence of feedback of the stochastic measurement record, deriving non-Markovian SDEs for the evolution of the projected state of the Markovian embedding. This paper generalizes these stochastic equations to the setting of stochastic feedback based on the continuous-measurement record and shows that the equations take the same form but that previously deterministic terms become stochastic ones which depend on the measurement record, as would be intuitively expected. The stochastic equations are obtained for a generalized class of measurements that includes continuous (possibly adaptive) homodyne and photon counting measurements.
one_liner: Projection-operator stochastic equations are extended to non-Markovian quantum systems with continuous measurement feedback.
why_it_matters: It supplies control equations needed when quantum optical, optomechanical, or circuit systems have memory but are still actively measured and fed back.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes projection-operator stochastic equations for continuously measured non-Markovian quantum systems to include feedback based on the measurement record. It treats the non-Markovian system through a larger Markovian embedding, then derives projected stochastic dynamics in which terms that were deterministic without feedback become record-dependent stochastic terms. The measurement class includes continuous adaptive homodyne detection and photon counting, making the equations relevant to controlled open quantum systems.
platform_or_system: continuously measured non-Markovian open quantum systems
main_result: It derives stochastic feedback equations for projected non-Markovian quantum states under measurement-based control.
application_angle: The formalism supports feedback design for quantum photonic, optomechanical, and superconducting systems where Markov approximations are inadequate.

title: The limits of erasure-based postselection for quantum error mitigation
abstract: In both classical and quantum error correction, heralded erasures are known to be easier to tolerate than unheralded general stochastic errors. Whilst an established benefit of loss-dominant quantum architectures such as photonic qubits, this fact has received renewed interest, with a pivot towards reconstructing other architectures to be erasure-dominant, such as dual-rail transmons. This work investigates exploiting these 'erasure qubits' in the near term by using postselection as a technique for error mitigation, wherein circuit shots detecting any erased qubits are discarded from the computational ensemble and repeated. Firstly, we outline a numerical framework for representing circuit-level erasure noise and present 'erado', an open-source library capable of simulating erasure noise and postselection. Secondly, we investigate the effects of both erasure noise and noise in the erasure checks themselves on the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), in the additional presence of gate depolarising noise. A worked example is provided of postselection fully mitigating against the erasure channel for erasure check error rates less than 3.0%. We also show how a postselected dual-rail system can surpass a fundamental noise floor at the kiloquop scale where a comparable single-rail system cannot, justifying this approach in the NISQ regime before (and, perhaps, combined with) the practical arrival of QEC.
one_liner: Analyzes when heralded erasure postselection can mitigate circuit noise in near-term erasure-qubit architectures.
why_it_matters: It quantifies a practical NISQ use case for erasure-biased hardware before full QEC, including dual-rail transmon-style systems.
detailed_summary: The paper builds a circuit-level numerical framework for erasure noise and introduces the open-source simulator erado. It studies QFT circuits with erasures, imperfect erasure checks, and depolarizing gate noise, showing full mitigation of the erasure channel when check errors stay below 3.0% in a worked example. It further argues that postselected dual-rail hardware can beat a kiloquop-scale noise floor inaccessible to comparable single-rail systems.
main_result: Postselection can fully remove the erasure-channel contribution under sufficiently accurate erasure checks and can improve kiloquop-scale performance versus single-rail hardware.
application_angle: The result gives hardware teams a concrete near-term mitigation strategy for loss- or erasure-dominant qubit platforms before large-scale error correction is available.

title: Plasmonic-cavity Modulator for the Mid-IR with a Semi-transparent and Nonlinear Heavily-doped Semiconductor Mirror
abstract: We present a free-space plasmonic modulator based on a single heavily-doped semiconductor layer. We investigate its ability to modulate both the linear and nonlinear response at mid-infrared frequencies slightly below the plasma frequency of the semiconductor. We demonstrate electric control of the linear transmittance and reflectance, and of the efficiency of third-harmonic generation with a field-effect gate structure. We discuss further performance optimization of the device in terms of modulation speed and depth towards a fast modulator with very simple active material requirements. Our results establish a viable route toward practical plasmonic modulators and mixers operating in the mid-infrared atmospheric window available for free-space communications at wavelengths between 8 and 12 um.
one_liner: Demonstrates an electrically gated mid-IR plasmonic modulator using a single heavily doped semiconductor layer.
why_it_matters: A simple active material stack that modulates linear and nonlinear mid-IR response is directly relevant to free-space optical links and mixers.
detailed_summary: The work presents a free-space plasmonic cavity modulator based on a heavily doped semiconductor layer operated near its plasma frequency. A field-effect gate controls transmittance, reflectance, and third-harmonic-generation efficiency. The paper also discusses optimization of speed and modulation depth for operation in the 8-12 um atmospheric window.
main_result: The device electrically modulates both linear optical response and nonlinear third-harmonic generation in the mid-infrared.
application_angle: Fast, compact mid-IR modulators and mixers could support practical free-space communication through atmospheric transmission windows.

title: Spectral Geometry and Bosonic-Bloch Probes: Explorations in Quantum Learning
abstract: This paper studies how spectral geometry emerges in quantum learning models and how it can be diagnosed with physically grounded probes. In graph-regularized quantum networks, training reorganizes the output similarity graph, increases the effective spectral dimension Delta S = +0.23, and reshapes the Laplacian spectrum. Edge-resolved two-boson interference directly probes this restructuring: the bosonic enhancement Delta P_uv correlates with the Fiedler edge split |Delta v_2| (r = -0.50), linking learned spectral partitions to interference signatures. A phase diagram shows a nonmonotonic dependence of performance on coupling strength gamma and noise delta, with graph regularization improving fidelity only in a restricted regime; hardware experiments confirm the predicted interference behavior within shot-noise uncertainty. We also analyze a hybrid quantum autoencoder and introduce Bloch-space drift as a geometric diagnostic of its latent representation. With an unsupervised benign-data threshold, the model achieves high ranking performance (ROC-AUC about 0.99) and negligible false-negative rates. Absolute Bloch drift strongly discriminates anomalies (ROC-AUC at least about 0.9), while consecutive drift is near random (ROC-AUC about 0.5), showing that detection arises from persistent state-space displacement rather than local fluctuations. Through the geometry of reduced single-qubit states and associated quantum Fisher information, these results show that learning-induced spectral organization appears as measurable quantum-state structure, establishing a unified spectral-geometric framework for diagnosing quantum learning systems with bosonic and Bloch probes.
one_liner: Uses bosonic interference and Bloch-space drift as physical probes of learned geometry in quantum learning models.
why_it_matters: It links quantum ML behavior to measurable state and interference observables, including hardware-confirmed signatures within shot noise.
detailed_summary: The paper studies graph-regularized quantum networks and shows that training reshapes output similarity graphs, Laplacian spectra, and effective spectral dimension. Edge-resolved two-boson interference probes this restructuring, with bosonic enhancement correlated to Fiedler edge splits and hardware experiments matching predictions within shot-noise uncertainty. It also analyzes a hybrid quantum autoencoder where absolute Bloch-space drift separates anomalies with high ROC-AUC, while consecutive drift is near random.
platform_or_system: quantum learning circuits with bosonic and Bloch probes
main_result: Learning-induced spectral organization is shown to appear as measurable interference patterns and persistent single-qubit state-space displacement.
application_angle: The diagnostics could help validate, debug, and monitor quantum learning systems on real hardware using physically accessible observables.

title: Resourcefulness without Resource: Geometric Origins and Robustness
abstract: A prevailing intuition holds that quantum protocols using only free states confer no operational advantage. This intuition is contradicted by free-state discrimination gaps in which restricted measurements fail to optimally distinguish even orthogonal free states. Known instances include nonlocality without entanglement and, more recently, nonstabilizerness without magic. We trace these examples to a single convex-geometric mechanism: whenever the set of free measurements is closed, convex, and strict subset the set of all measurements, and the free states is a convex set with an interior, a gap-witnessing ensemble can be drawn entirely from the free states. The resulting gap is operationally rigid: no finite-dimensional assistance -- catalyst or quantum memory -- can asymptotically improve the discrimination rate beyond the single-shot restricted limit. By contrast, non-free ensembles admit memory-assisted attacks that fully erase the gap, exposing a sharp operational asymmetry between free and resource-carrying ensembles.
one_liner: Identifies a convex-geometric mechanism behind operational advantages obtained using only free states.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when restricted measurements create discrimination gaps, a foundation relevant to quantum protocol design and resource certification.
detailed_summary: The paper unifies examples such as nonlocality without entanglement and nonstabilizerness without magic through a convex-geometric condition on free states and free measurements. When free measurements are a closed convex strict subset of all measurements and the free-state set has interior, an all-free ensemble can witness a discrimination gap. The gap is rigid against finite-dimensional catalysts or quantum memory, while non-free ensembles can lose the gap under memory-assisted attacks.
main_result: Free-state ensembles can exhibit robust operational discrimination advantages whenever the allowed measurement set is sufficiently restricted.
application_angle: The result informs communication and certification protocols where measurement restrictions, not only state resources, determine achievable performance.

title: Machine Learning based Optimization of CV-QKD Under Practical Constraints
abstract: Practical hardware limitations, including finite transmitter and receiver filter lengths as well as the finite resolution of digital-to-analog and analog-to-digital converters, lead to mode mismatch and degrade the performance of continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems. To address this, we develop a machine learning-based end-to-end optimization framework that jointly optimizes transmitter pulse shaping and receiver matched filtering. The approach employs reinforcement learning under realistic hardware constraints, including a limited number of filter taps, finite digital-to-analog and analog-to-digital converter resolution, analog low-pass filtering, and the optimal mean photon number. By mitigating mode mismatch and accounting for implementation constraints, the proposed method improves overall system performance. Simulation results demonstrate enhanced secure key rates compared to conventional approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
one_liner: Applies reinforcement learning to jointly optimize pulse shaping and matched filtering for practical CV-QKD systems.
why_it_matters: It targets real hardware bottlenecks such as finite filter taps, converter resolution, analog filtering, and mode mismatch that limit secure key rates.
detailed_summary: The paper develops an end-to-end machine-learning framework for continuous-variable QKD under implementation constraints. It jointly optimizes transmitter pulse shaping, receiver matched filtering, and mean photon number while modeling finite DAC/ADC resolution, limited filter lengths, and analog low-pass filtering. Simulations show higher secure key rates than conventional designs by reducing mode mismatch under realistic constraints.
main_result: The RL-based optimizer improves simulated secure key rates for constrained CV-QKD hardware compared with standard pulse and filter choices.
application_angle: This is a practical design workflow for squeezing more key rate from deployable CV-QKD equipment without assuming ideal electronics.

title: Inverse-squeezing receivers for squeezed-state pulse-position modulation under ideal and phase-diffusion conditions
abstract: We introduce a squeezed-state pulse-position modulation (S-PPM) format, where the empty slots are squeezed vacuum states and the pulse slot is a displaced squeezed state. Based on this property, we propose an inverse-squeezing conditional pulse-nulling (IS-CPN) receiver. In the ideal case, inverse squeezing maps S-PPM into an equivalent coherent-state PPM signal with a large pulse energy, leading to a closed-form expression for the receiver error probability. We further analyze IS-CPN under common phase diffusion using a finite-path MAP formulation with phase-averaged likelihoods. Numerical results show that IS-CPN outperforms conventional CPN under the same energy constraint and remains advantageous under phase noise and finite photon-number resolution. These results demonstrate that combining squeezed-state modulation with inverse-squeezing conditional nulling can improve photon-efficient optical communication.
one_liner: Proposes inverse-squeezing conditional pulse nulling for photon-efficient squeezed-state PPM receivers.
why_it_matters: It combines squeezed modulation and receiver-side inverse squeezing to improve optical communication sensitivity under realistic phase noise.
detailed_summary: The paper defines squeezed-state pulse-position modulation, where empty slots are squeezed vacuum and the pulse slot is a displaced squeezed state. Its inverse-squeezing conditional pulse-nulling receiver maps ideal S-PPM into an equivalent coherent-state PPM signal with enhanced pulse energy and admits a closed-form error expression. Under common phase diffusion, a finite-path MAP treatment with phase-averaged likelihoods shows advantage over conventional CPN even with phase noise and finite photon-number resolution.
main_result: Inverse-squeezing CPN lowers detection error versus conventional CPN under equal energy constraints, including noisy phase-diffusion settings.
application_angle: The scheme could improve photon-efficient optical links where receiver sensitivity and robustness to phase noise are limiting factors.

title: Signatures of the circular Unruh effect in electric and magnetic dipole transitions of multilevel atoms
abstract: The circular Unruh effect is the excitation of a detector moving along a planar circular trajectory within an electromagnetic vacuum. We demonstrate that the magnetic dipole transitions in an atom, acting as the detector, dominate the electric dipole transitions. Our analysis of both free-space and cavity schemes shows that the sensitivity to the circular Unruh effect can be maximized by balancing the minimization of mode volume against the resulting decrease in mode density. Moreover, we propose a novel measurement scheme that uses the atom's multilevel structure to suppress the spontaneous emission rate, thereby enabling the experimental detection of the circular Unruh effect.
one_liner: Multilevel atoms are proposed as detectors for circular Unruh signatures using magnetic-dipole dominated transitions.
why_it_matters: It outlines an experimentally motivated route to observing acceleration-induced vacuum effects by suppressing spontaneous emission in atomic systems.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes atoms on circular trajectories as electromagnetic-vacuum detectors and finds magnetic dipole transitions can dominate electric dipole channels. It compares free-space and cavity-assisted schemes, showing sensitivity depends on the tradeoff between small mode volume and reduced mode density. A multilevel-atom protocol is proposed to suppress spontaneous emission and make the circular Unruh signal experimentally accessible.
platform_or_system: multilevel atomic detector in free space or cavity
main_result: The study identifies magnetic-dipole transitions and multilevel suppression of spontaneous emission as key ingredients for detecting circular Unruh signatures.
application_angle: The proposed measurement architecture could turn relativistic quantum-vacuum effects into a testable signal in controlled atomic or cavity systems.

title: Distributed Property Testing with (Quantum) Carrier Pigeons: Tight Bounds on State Certification
abstract: Recently, Doosti et al. introduced the problem of distributed quantum state verification, where $m$ distributed nodes are given a copy of an unknown state $ρ$, and can send limited one way communication to a central node, who has a complete description of a known state $σ$. They ask how many distributed nodes $m$ are required, before the central node can succeed at distinguishing whether $ρ=σ$ or $\|ρ-σ\|_1\geq\varepsilon$ with high probability. In the setting where only quantum communication is allowed, Doosti et al. exhibit conditional lower bounds in both the public and private-coin settings, and a matching upper bound in the public-coin setting. We extend these results, and show unconditional lower bounds for when both classical and quantum communication are permitted. We show the public-coin lower bound is tight by giving an algorithm with a matching upper bound. We also show an almost tight upper bound in the private-coin setting when only quantum communication is permitted.
one_liner: The paper proves tight communication bounds for distributed quantum state certification with classical and quantum messages.
why_it_matters: It clarifies the resource cost of verifying quantum states across distributed nodes, relevant to networked quantum processors and communication protocols.
detailed_summary: The work studies how many distributed copies of an unknown quantum state are needed when nodes send limited one-way information to a central verifier. It gives unconditional lower bounds when both classical and quantum communication are allowed, strengthening earlier conditional results. It also provides matching public-coin upper bounds and nearly tight private-coin upper bounds for quantum-only communication.
main_result: The paper establishes tight or nearly tight bounds for distributed quantum state certification under multiple communication models.
application_angle: These limits inform how much communication and replication are needed for practical verification in quantum networks and distributed quantum computing.

title: Context-Verified, Error-Budget-Aware Decomposition Selection for Toffoli Networks
abstract: Two-qubit-gate error dominates the failure budget of near-term quantum circuits, so the decomposition chosen for each Toffoli (CCX) gate should minimize hardware two-qubit infidelity, not gate count. The cheapest decompositions - relative-phase and approximate Toffolis - are only correct in context: their residual phase or bounded error must be cancelled or absorbed downstream. We present the first compiler pass that selects a per-Toffoli decomposition to minimize a two-qubit-infidelity error budget. It admits each context-dependent decomposition only when an exact, instance-specific equivalence check certifies its validity in that circuit context, coupling an error-budget objective with per-instance verification and closing the gap between context-aware-but-unverified and verified-but-context-free optimizers. The central result is a safety one: pattern-matched relative-phase substitution is silently incorrect. Our verifier flags 66 library rewrites of a deployed open optimizer as non-equivalent without a context check, and count-greedy substitution silently corrupts 6 of 12 benchmark circuits; the verification gate certifies 0 errors while still applying every valid decomposition. The two-qubit-gate reduction is real but workload-dependent: up to 39.5% fewer two-qubit gates and 36.7% lower infidelity over exact-only on a compute/uncompute-heavy suite (approx. 39%/35% versus Qiskit opt-3 and tket), and 15.6% aggregate on a larger 12-24-qubit suite, with decision-diagram checking certifying every substitution past the exhaustive-verification limit. At current superconducting and trapped-ion error rates, the certified substitutions lower estimated circuit infidelity by 36-43%, and on a quantum state-resetting circuit, the pass removes 48.8% of the native two-qubit gates, every substitution verified.
one_liner: A compiler pass safely chooses per-Toffoli decompositions using context verification and hardware error budgets.
why_it_matters: It shows that aggressive Toffoli rewrites can silently corrupt circuits unless each context-dependent substitution is formally checked.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a compiler pass that selects exact, relative-phase, or approximate Toffoli decompositions according to two-qubit-gate infidelity rather than raw gate count. Each context-dependent rewrite is admitted only after an instance-specific equivalence check, preventing invalid substitutions that pattern matching would allow. Benchmarks show substantial two-qubit-gate and estimated infidelity reductions, with decision-diagram verification certifying all accepted rewrites.
main_result: The pass achieves up to 39.5% fewer two-qubit gates and 36-43% lower estimated infidelity while certifying every Toffoli substitution.
application_angle: Verified hardware-aware decomposition can improve near-term circuit fidelity without accepting compiler-induced correctness risk.

title: Correlation-enhanced metrology from scrambling dynamics in a solid-state spin system
abstract: Quantum information scrambling, the dispersal of local information into many-body degrees of freedom, provides a powerful mechanism for generating large-scale correlations and entanglement essential for quantum-enhanced metrology. However, experimentally verifying such quantum-enhanced metrology remains a demanding task. Here, we correlate thousands of spins by engineering chaotic scrambling dynamics in a solid-state nuclear spin system. By leveraging the newly developed scramblon theory, we reveal exponential scaling in both the quantum Fisher information and the signal response to a phase shift. The signal response achieves a correlation-enabled enhancement of $33(2)$ dB over uncorrelated spins. After accounting for signal loss due to imperfect time reversal in the readout stage, we obtain a total metrological gain of 18(1) dB with a phase sensitivity of 40(3) ${\mathrm{μrad}}$. Our results bridge quantum chaos with practical quantum metrology, establishing reversible scrambling dynamics as a powerful resource for precision measurements.
one_liner: Chaotic scrambling dynamics correlate thousands of solid-state nuclear spins for enhanced quantum metrology.
why_it_matters: It experimentally links many-body scrambling to large metrological gain, moving quantum chaos from theory toward precision sensing.
detailed_summary: The experiment engineers chaotic reversible dynamics in a solid-state nuclear spin ensemble to spread local information into many-body correlations. Using scramblon theory, the authors observe exponential scaling of both quantum Fisher information and phase-response signal. The measured response gives 33(2) dB correlation-enabled enhancement and an 18(1) dB total metrological gain after imperfect readout reversal is included.
main_result: The system reaches 40(3) microradian phase sensitivity with 18(1) dB total metrological gain from scrambling-generated correlations.
application_angle: Reversible scrambling could become a practical resource for high-sensitivity solid-state phase, field, or frequency sensors.

title: Lazy-Move Compilation for Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers via a Buffer-Relay Fabric
abstract: Neutral atom quantum computing offers strong scalability and flexible qubit connectivity, but most existing compilation flows rely on reconfigurable atom arrays that physically shuttle qubit atoms during execution. Although this approach improves connectivity, it also introduces handoff errors, motional heating, and atom-loss risks that can degrade overall fidelity. We present BRIDGE, a Buffer-Relay Interconnect for Data-stable Gate Execution that co-designs a static, compiler-managed buffer-relay fabric with a lazy-move compiler that exploits it. BRIDGE targets an optimized, dual-species 2D interleaved atom array, using non-encoding ``buffer atoms'' to mediate long-range interactions in the fixed baseline and introducing limited data motion only for selected hotspots. By using calibrated heteronuclear and homonuclear Rydberg channels, BRIDGE realizes a static routing backbone in which data-buffer and buffer-buffer interactions are enabled while residual data-data crosstalk is suppressed. Across a 22-circuit matched benchmark suite re-estimated under a single shared error model, BRIDGE attains a geometric-mean $\sim$10$\times$ higher total fidelity than ZAP and $\sim$16$\times$ than Enola, together with $\sim$540$\times$ and $\sim$1000$\times$ lower circuit execution time, respectively, while reducing data-atom movement from thousands of transport events to zero.
one_liner: BRIDGE uses static buffer-relay atoms and lazy movement to improve neutral-atom compilation fidelity and runtime.
why_it_matters: It targets a core neutral-atom bottleneck: maintaining connectivity while avoiding atom transport errors, heating, and loss.
detailed_summary: The paper presents BRIDGE, a co-designed neutral-atom architecture and compiler using non-encoding buffer atoms as a static relay fabric. A dual-species interleaved array enables calibrated heteronuclear and homonuclear Rydberg channels while suppressing residual data-data crosstalk. On a matched benchmark suite under a shared error model, BRIDGE improves geometric-mean total fidelity by about 10x versus ZAP and 16x versus Enola while eliminating thousands of data-atom moves.
